title-group.article-title: From Natural Language to Verifiable GeoWorkflows: A Typed LLM-Orchestration Framework for Predictive Geodata Science

article-meta.aff: Vietnam National University Ho Chi Minh City – Ben Tre Campus, Vinh Long, Vietnam

abstract.p: Natural-language interfaces can lower the expertise barrier to geospatial analysis, but direct prompt-to-code systems remain vulnerable to silent errors in coordinate reference systems, units, temporal alignment, data provenance, topology, and model selection. This paper presents GeoPlan, a verifiable framework that treats a large language model (LLM) as a semantic planner and workflow compiler rather than as the numerical authority for geometry or prediction. GeoPlan translates an analyst's request into GeoPlan-IR, a typed directed acyclic graph that explicitly records spatial entities, coordinate systems, units, temporal extents, data lineage, uncertainty, model assumptions, and acceptance constraints. A spatial knowledge graph grounds domain concepts and data catalogs; static and dynamic verifiers check the plan before and after execution; and sandboxed adapters compile approved plans to PostGIS, Python geospatial libraries, or Google Earth Engine. The paper further specifies GeoNL2Workflow, an expert-annotated benchmark covering vector, raster, network, spatiotemporal, predictive, and streaming Internet-of-Things tasks. Evaluation separates semantic fidelity, plan correctness, executability, result agreement, robustness, safety, and resource cost rather than collapsing them into a single code-generation score. Two reproducible case studies are defined: compound-flood susceptibility under SSP2-4.5 conditions using satellite, climate, and ESP32 sensor streams, and land-use change prediction from multitemporal Earth observation data. The prespecified primary success criterion is at least 85% end-to-end valid workflow generation on held-out tasks relative to expert reference workflows; it is a target, not a reported empirical result. The framework's central contribution is a neurosymbolic contract between language and geocomputation that makes LLM-assisted predictive geodata science inspectable, portable, and suitable for human-governed decision support.

sec.title: 1 Introduction
sec.p: Geographic information science is moving from descriptive mapping toward predictive geodata science: analysts increasingly combine Earth observation, spatial databases, simulation, machine learning, and live sensor streams to estimate what may happen, where, when, and with what uncertainty. Yet the operational interface to this ecosystem remains fragmented. A seemingly simple question about flood exposure may require data discovery, coordinate transformation, temporal harmonization, hydrological conditioning, feature engineering, model selection, validation, and cartographic communication. Each step introduces domain assumptions that are rarely visible to non-specialists and are easy to mishandle even when generated code executes successfully.

LLM-based GIS agents offer a compelling interaction model because they can decompose natural-language requests, retrieve documentation, call tools, and generate code. Early systems such as LLM-Geo, GeoGPT, and GIS Copilot demonstrated that language models can orchestrate common geoprocessing operations [3-5]. More recent multi-agent and benchmark studies show meaningful gains but also a persistent complexity ceiling: success deteriorates as tasks require more tools, heterogeneous data, ambiguous constraints, or predictive reasoning [6-10]. Intrinsic topological reasoning is itself unreliable; experiments with well-known text geometries report only moderate accuracy and emphasize that spatial databases remain more competent at exact computation [11]. These findings expose a central design mistake in many prototypes: an executable script is treated as evidence of a correct spatial analysis.

This paper addresses the gap between linguistic plausibility and geocomputational validity. We propose GeoPlan, a framework in which the LLM performs semantic interpretation, constrained planning, and explanation, while deterministic spatial engines perform geometry, statistics, simulation, and prediction. The boundary between these roles is encoded in a typed intermediate representation called GeoPlan-IR. Instead of asking a model to emit unrestricted Python, the system first produces a machine-checkable workflow graph containing explicit data contracts and spatial invariants. This design makes errors such as buffering longitude-latitude coordinates in metres, joining observations from incompatible timestamps, or fitting a predictive model with spatial leakage detectable before execution.

Research questions. RQ1 asks whether ontology-grounded GeoPlan-IR improves semantic and structural workflow correctness compared with direct prompt-to-code and unconstrained tool calling. RQ2 asks how much static and dynamic verification reduces silent spatial errors while preserving task completion. RQ3 asks whether the framework generalizes across geography, data modality, and application domain, including live edge-IoT observations.
The paper makes four contributions:

list-item.p: A typed, model-agnostic intermediate representation for natural-language-to-geospatial workflows, including coordinate systems, units, time, scale, uncertainty, provenance, and acceptance constraints.
A verification architecture that combines ontology grounding, static plan checks, sandboxed execution, result invariants, bounded repair, and human escalation.
A benchmark and evaluation protocol that distinguishes semantic fidelity, graph correctness, functional execution, output equivalence, robustness, safety, and computational cost.
Two end-to-end predictive case-study specifications connecting cloud geocomputation with satellite products and georeferenced ESP32 sensor streams.

sec.title: 2.1 From GIS automation to agentic geocomputation
sec.p: Autonomous GIS has been framed as a progression toward systems that can generate, organize, verify, execute, and improve geospatial workflows [3]. LLM-Geo represents workflows as solution graphs and generates executable programs; GeoGPT similarly combines natural-language understanding with a tool registry [4]. GIS Copilot integrates an informed agent into QGIS and evaluates more than one hundred tasks at several complexity levels [5]. These systems established feasibility, but their primary abstraction remains code or a loosely typed tool sequence. Consequently, the burden of validating spatial semantics often remains outside the agent.

Mansourian and Oucheikh introduced a multi-agent QGIS framework with retrieval, fine-tuning, and specialized roles [6]. The study reported high execution success on short workflows but reduced effectiveness as complexity increased. GISclaw extends coverage across vector, raster, and tabular analysis and highlights an important systems result: additional agent layers do not automatically improve strong models and may introduce coordination overhead [10]. GeoPlan therefore avoids assuming that more agents imply better reasoning. It uses a small number of explicit compiler and verifier roles whose outputs are typed, observable, and independently testable.

sec.title: 2.2 Benchmarks and the functional-equivalence problem
sec.p: GeoAnalystBench contains 50 expert-validated Python tasks and calls for rigorous evaluation before claims of full GIS automation [7]. Bench4GeoCode contributes 100 progressively difficult tasks, including unattainable and ambiguous queries, and separates functional correctness from code quality [8]. These benchmarks are important, yet predictive geodata science adds requirements that code execution alone cannot capture: the same analysis can be implemented by different valid workflows; conversely, two scripts may run and produce maps while embodying incompatible coordinate systems, temporal definitions, leakage controls, or uncertainty assumptions. GeoPlan evaluates equivalence at plan, execution, and result levels and records acceptable alternative workflows in the gold standard.

sec.title: 2.3 Spatial semantics, standards, and exact computation
sec.p: GeoSPARQL provides vocabularies and query functions for representing geospatial entities, geometries, and topological relations in RDF [12, 13]. The SpatioTemporal Asset Catalog specification supplies a common structure for describing and discovering Earth-observation assets [14]. W3C PROV-O and SHACL support data lineage and graph validation [15, 16]. These standards enable a neurosymbolic architecture: language is grounded to formal concepts, constraints are validated symbolically, and exact geometry is delegated to databases and geospatial libraries. The framework consequently interprets an LLM as a spatial reasoning orchestrator, not as a replacement for DE-9IM predicates, raster algebra, hydrodynamic models, or calibrated statistical learners.

sec.title: 2.4 Research gap and novelty
sec.p: The closest published title to the initial framing of this study is the 2026 multi-agent work in [6]. GeoPlan is differentiated technically and rhetorically: it does not claim novelty merely from bridging language and GIS. Its contribution is the typed contract that separates semantic planning from numerical execution, plus verification criteria tailored to predictive and streaming geodata.
Table 1. Positioning of GeoPlan relative to representative LLM-GIS approaches.

tr.td: Static, dynamic, result and policy checks
Raster, vector, prediction and edge-IoT streams

sec.title: 3 Problem Formulation
sec.p: Let a user request be q, contextual information be C, available datasets and catalogs be D, and authorized execution environments be E. The system must produce a workflow W = (V, A), where V is a set of typed operations and A is a set of data-dependency edges. A workflow is acceptable only if it is semantically faithful to q, well typed with respect to D, executable within E, and demonstrably consistent with output constraints. The objective is not exact textual or code match. It is constrained functional equivalence: multiple plans may be valid if they satisfy the same intent, preconditions, invariants, and tolerance-bounded outputs.

We define a workflow utility U(W) = alpha S_sem + beta S_plan + gamma S_out - lambda R - mu C, where S_sem is semantic fidelity, S_plan is typed graph correctness, S_out is result agreement, R is safety and epistemic risk, and C is normalized computational cost. The coefficients are fixed before evaluation and sensitivity analysis reports whether conclusions depend on a particular weighting. Primary claims are based on the component measures rather than U(W), preventing a high score in one dimension from concealing a critical failure in another.

Spatial correctness. A plan is spatially correct when geometry types, coordinate reference systems, units, spatial scale, topology, temporal support, resolution, and boundary semantics are explicitly defined or safely inferred and then validated. Terms such as near, upstream, coastal corridor, recent, or high risk are treated as underspecified until resolved by policy, domain context, or user clarification.

Predictive correctness. A predictive plan additionally specifies target variables, forecasting horizon, feature availability at prediction time, spatial and temporal cross-validation, leakage controls, calibration, uncertainty outputs, and a reproducible model-selection protocol. The LLM may recommend a model family, but only models registered with machine-readable preconditions can be executed automatically.

sec.title: 4 GeoPlan Framework

graphic.xlink:title: GeoPlan architecture
graphic.alt-text: A seven-stage flow converts a natural-language spatial task into a grounded typed plan, verifies it, executes it in deterministic geospatial engines, checks outputs, and returns a decision-ready result with provenance and human controls.

sec.title: 4.1 Design principles
sec.p: GeoPlan follows five principles. First, semantic planning is separated from execution. Second, every automatic inference that can change a result is made explicit in GeoPlan-IR. Third, data and tools are discovered through registries rather than recalled from model parameters. Fourth, verification is layered: cheap static checks precede costly execution, and result checks precede release. Fifth, the system escalates ambiguity and high-impact decisions to a human instead of forcing completion. This final principle is essential for trustworthy automation because a correct response to an ill-posed request may be a clarification question or a documented refusal.

sec.title: 4.2 GeoPlan-IR: a typed intermediate representation
sec.p: GeoPlan-IR is serialized as JSON or RDF but is conceptually a typed DAG. Each node declares its operation, inputs, outputs, parameter types, spatial and temporal contracts, preconditions, postconditions, and evidence. The graph is model agnostic and platform neutral: the same plan can be compiled to SQL/PostGIS, a Python stack, or Earth Engine when equivalent operators are available.
Table 2. Core GeoPlan-IR fields and the failures they are designed to prevent.

tr.td: task type, decision purpose, target, horizon
geometry type, CRS, extent, resolution, scale, units
Invalid distance, area, overlay, or resampling
event time, interval, timezone, aggregation, lag
schema, source, licence, quality, lineage, access
Incorrect tool order or incompatible data types
target, features, split, model, calibration, uncertainty
tests, tolerances, risk tier, human approval
Release of plausible but invalid outputs

sec.p: A minimal buffer node, for example, cannot contain only a distance value. It must identify an input geometry, output geometry, projected CRS or geodesic method, unit, cap and join policy, invalid-geometry handling, and postconditions such as non-empty output and preserved feature identifiers. This explicitness converts many GIS best practices into compile-time checks.

sec.title: 4.3 Semantic grounding and data discovery
sec.p: The grounding layer maps place names, domain phrases, and vague relations to canonical entities and predicates. A spatial knowledge graph combines GeoSPARQL relations with domain ontologies for hydrology, land cover, urban zoning, hazards, and sensors. It also links concepts to tool signatures and catalog assets. Retrieval is constrained by geographic coverage, time span, resolution, licensing, update frequency, and authorization. STAC records identify raster assets; database catalogs expose vector and tabular schemas; sensor registries expose station coordinates, units, calibration dates, and quality flags.

Ambiguity is quantified rather than hidden. If coastal corridor could refer to an administrative buffer, an elevation-defined coastal zone, or a distance from shoreline, the system returns candidate interpretations with consequences for data and output. An automatic choice is permitted only when an organization-approved default exists and its use is recorded in the plan.

sec.title: 4.4 Planning, compilation, and bounded repair
sec.p: The planner decomposes q into data acquisition, preprocessing, analysis, prediction, validation, and presentation nodes. Retrieval supplies only tool documentation and examples compatible with the current execution environment. The compiler then resolves abstract operators to concrete implementations. For instance, spatial_join may compile to ST_Intersects in PostGIS, GeoPandas.sjoin in Python, or an Earth Engine join. Platform-specific code is generated from typed operator templates, reducing the unconstrained code surface.

When a verifier rejects a plan or execution fails, the system may enter a bounded repair loop. The error, relevant schema, and failed invariant are returned to the planner; unrelated context and raw secrets are withheld. Repair is limited by attempt count, cost budget, and risk tier. Repeated failure, missing data, or an ambiguous high-impact assumption triggers human escalation. This differs from open-ended self-debugging because the permissible state transitions are explicit and auditable.

sec.title: 4.5 Static, execution, and result verification
sec.p: Static verification uses JSON Schema or SHACL shapes, operator signatures, and domain rules. It checks DAG acyclicity, type compatibility, CRS and unit consistency, temporal ordering, required metadata, tool authorization, and model preconditions. Predictive rules flag random train-test splits for strongly spatial data, features unavailable at forecast time, fitting preprocessing outside cross-validation, and missing calibration or uncertainty outputs.

Execution occurs in a sandbox with read-only inputs, explicit output locations, resource quotas, network allowlists, and parameterized SQL. Dynamic checks inspect geometry validity, row and pixel counts, missingness, spatial bounds, temporal coverage, and distribution shifts. Result verification compares outputs with reference tests or invariant-based expectations. Examples include conservation of total area within tolerance after reprojection, monotonicity of cumulative inundation area with increasing water level, and agreement between independently implemented spatial predicates.

Every released artifact carries a provenance bundle: normalized request, GeoPlan-IR, model and tool versions, dataset identifiers and checksums, generated code, runtime log, verification results, uncertainty summary, and human interventions. This bundle supports reproduction, audit, and post-hoc comparison when models or datasets change.

sec.title: 5.1 Dataset construction
sec.p: GeoNL2Workflow is designed as an expert-authored benchmark rather than a collection of automatically paraphrased coding prompts. Candidate tasks are elicited from GIS analysts, remote-sensing specialists, hydrologists, planners, and IoT engineers. Each task is independently formalized by two annotators and adjudicated by a third. The released unit contains the natural-language request, ambiguity labels, required clarifications, admissible data sources, one or more gold GeoPlan-IR graphs, executable reference implementations, test fixtures, expected invariants, and risk classification.

The planned corpus contains 1,200 tasks: 720 core tasks, 240 robustness tasks, 120 predictive tasks, and 120 streaming or edge-IoT tasks. These counts are design targets and must be replaced by achieved counts in the empirical submission. Tasks are stratified by operation count and dependency depth. Gold alternatives capture scientifically equivalent algorithms within declared tolerances.
Table 3. Planned benchmark taxonomy.

tr.td: buffer, overlay, spatial join, dissolve, network
CRS, units, invalid geometry, predicate confusion
mask, composite, index, resample, zonal statistics
scale, projection, cloud masking, temporal mismatch

MQTT ingest, calibration, quality control, spatial fusion
clock drift, units, sensor relocation, dropout
ambiguity, impossible request, missing data, policy conflict

sec.title: 5.2 Leakage-resistant splits and perturbations
sec.p: Random prompt splits are insufficient because templates, place names, and code idioms can leak across partitions. GeoNL2Workflow uses four held-out regimes: geographic holdout, in which regions in the test set are absent from training; operator-composition holdout, in which known operations occur in novel combinations; temporal holdout, in which later data versions are used only for testing; and domain holdout, in which an application such as coastal flooding is evaluated after training on other hazards. Robustness variants perturb CRS metadata, units, schema names, incomplete temporal ranges, unavailable data, and conflicting instructions.

Ambiguous tasks are scored correct only if the system asks an information-bearing clarification or selects a documented default. Trap tasks are scored correct when the system identifies that the request cannot be satisfied with the authorized data and tools. These cases prevent completion rate from becoming a proxy for quality.

sec.title: 6.1 Systems and ablations
sec.p: All model identifiers, weights, inference parameters, prompts, retrieval indexes, and tool versions will be frozen before the final evaluation. At least two open-weight model families and one strong hosted model will be tested under identical tool permissions. The following systems isolate the contribution of each architectural component.

list-item.p: B0 - direct natural-language-to-code generation without retrieval or tools.
B1 - retrieval-augmented code generation using GIS documentation.
B2 - unconstrained tool-calling agent with runtime feedback.
B3 - GeoPlan-IR without the spatial knowledge graph.
B4 - GeoPlan-IR plus knowledge-graph grounding but without verification.
P - full GeoPlan with grounding, static checks, sandbox execution, result verification, and bounded repair.

sec.p: Ablations remove CRS checks, temporal checks, provenance, predictive leakage rules, or result invariants one at a time. This design tests whether the framework improves scientific validity rather than merely adding orchestration overhead. Each stochastic configuration is repeated with prespecified seeds; tasks are executed in fresh containers to prevent state leakage.

sec.title: 6.2 Metrics
sec.p: Table 4. Evaluation dimensions and operational definitions.

tr.td: Match of target, geography, time, constraint, output and decision purpose
Graph match over acceptable gold workflows after canonicalization
Plans passing CRS, unit, time, schema and model preconditions
Completion in a fresh sandbox without manual code repair
Clarify, abstain or recover under ambiguity, traps and perturbations
Unauthorized data access, destructive command or unbounded resource request
Median and tail resource consumption per valid task

sec.p: The primary endpoint is end-to-end valid workflow generation: a task counts as successful only when semantic fidelity, contract validity, clean execution, and result agreement all pass. The prespecified target is at least 0.85 on held-out tasks with a two-sided 95% Wilson confidence interval. Secondary endpoints include each component metric, calibration error for predictive outputs, human correction time, and cost per valid task. The unsafe execution target is below 0.05, but any high-severity event is reported separately and cannot be averaged away.

sec.title: 6.3 Statistical analysis and human evaluation
sec.p: Paired system comparisons use task-level McNemar tests for binary success and paired bootstrap confidence intervals for continuous scores. Holm correction controls family-wise error across planned comparisons. Mixed-effects logistic regression estimates the effects of architecture, model family, task depth, modality, and holdout regime while treating task as a random effect. Human experts evaluate a stratified blind sample for semantic adequacy, scientific defensibility, trace usefulness, and correction effort. Inter-rater agreement is reported with Krippendorff's alpha or an appropriate weighted coefficient.

LLM-as-judge ratings, if used, are secondary and calibrated against experts; they never replace execution tests or spatial result comparison. Error analysis assigns failures to interpretation, data discovery, planning, parameterization, code, execution environment, verification, or explanation. Reporting the distribution of failure types is necessary to distinguish model limits from infrastructure defects.

sec.title: 7.1 Compound-flood susceptibility under SSP2-4.5
sec.p: The first case study begins with the request: 'Identify coastal urban corridors with high compound-flood susceptibility in 2050 under SSP2-4.5, explain the dominant drivers, and produce an uncertainty-aware priority map.' The framework must clarify the study boundary, forecast window, definition of corridor, acceptable resolution, and decision use. Candidate data include Sentinel-1 flood observations, Sentinel-2 or Landsat land cover, a digital elevation model, drainage and river networks, rainfall and reanalysis variables, tide or water-level records, urban exposure layers, and downscaled ScenarioMIP variables [20-23].

A network of ESP32 edge nodes can contribute georeferenced water level, rainfall, soil moisture, and local pressure. Each message includes sensor identifier, coordinates or station version, event timestamp, unit, calibration metadata, sequence number, and quality flags. Edge preprocessing performs range checks, timestamp normalization, simple filtering, and store-and-forward delivery. GeoPlan does not assume that sensor streams are ground truth: it creates explicit quality-control and spatial-fusion nodes and preserves raw-to-derived lineage.

The gold plan uses spatially blocked and temporally forward validation. Candidate predictive models may include gradient-boosted trees and spatiotemporal neural networks, but selection is based on a registered protocol rather than LLM preference. Evaluation reports discrimination, calibration, spatial transfer, uncertainty coverage, and agreement of priority zones with an expert pipeline. Physical plausibility checks require susceptibility to respond consistently to water-level and rainfall perturbations within the model's stated domain.

sec.title: 7.2 Land-use change prediction
sec.p: The second case study asks the system to predict land-use transitions and identify development pressure near transport corridors while respecting protected areas. Multitemporal Sentinel-2 or Landsat composites, existing land-cover products, road networks, planning zones, terrain, and settlement indicators are discovered through catalog constraints. The plan must distinguish land cover from land use, define the transition interval, harmonize legends, mask clouds, specify spatial resolution, and prevent the use of post-outcome covariates.

Reference workflows include a transparent baseline and a stronger predictive model evaluated with geographic holdouts. Result agreement is measured for transition probabilities, class-specific area, hotspot overlap, and ranking of pressure zones. Because a policy map can influence real decisions, GeoPlan must expose protected-area exclusions, uncertain classifications, and the sensitivity of results to alternative development assumptions.
Table 5. Case-study outputs and verification emphasis.

tr.td: susceptibility surface, drivers, uncertainty, priority corridors
time/CRS alignment, sensor QC, leakage, calibration, physical plausibility
transition probabilities, hotspots, scenario map, explanations
legend harmonization, geographic holdout, protected-area policy, uncertainty

sec.title: 8.1 Why a typed compiler is more defensible than prompt-to-code
sec.p: The scientific value of GeoPlan lies less in generating code than in making assumptions inspectable. Natural language is deliberately tolerant of vagueness, while spatial computation is not. A typed intermediate representation provides a negotiation layer between the two: it preserves the accessibility of conversational interaction but requires machine-checkable commitments before an operation becomes executable. This approach also reduces dependence on a particular model or GIS platform. New LLMs can be compared on plan generation, while new executors can be certified against the same operator contracts.

The framework also reframes spatial reasoning. LLMs are useful for mapping goals to concepts, decomposing tasks, recognizing missing information, retrieving procedures, and explaining outcomes. Exact geometry, raster algebra, optimization, and statistical estimation remain the responsibility of tested computational engines. This division of labor is consistent with evidence that LLM topological reasoning is imperfect [11] and avoids a category error in which linguistic confidence is mistaken for numerical validity.

sec.title: 8.2 Human-centered automation and trust
sec.p: Democratization should not mean removing experts from consequential decisions. GeoPlan supports graded autonomy. Low-risk exploratory tasks may execute automatically after all checks pass. Medium-risk tasks require approval of assumptions and datasets. High-risk outputs, such as public flood warnings or regulatory zoning recommendations, require expert review of the plan, uncertainty, and provenance. Trust is therefore attached to evidence and control points, not to anthropomorphic confidence.

Natural-language accessibility can broaden interdisciplinary participation, particularly when hydrologists, planners, local authorities, and sensor engineers need to collaborate. However, accessible interfaces may also conceal data gaps and uneven geographic representation. The benchmark therefore includes low-resource geographies, incomplete metadata, multilingual place references, and infrastructure constraints. Performance must be disaggregated by region and task type rather than reported as a single global average.

sec.title: 8.3 Reproducibility, security, and sustainability
sec.p: Reproducibility requires more than publishing prompts. The complete execution bundle must identify data versions, spatial extents, model artifacts, library versions, random seeds, and verification outcomes. Security requires least-privilege execution, credential isolation, parameterized database access, package allowlists, and protection against prompt injection embedded in metadata or documents. Sustainability is measured through cost and energy proxies so that marginal accuracy gains can be assessed against computational expense. Open-weight models and local execution can reduce dependence on external services, but they do not remove the need for versioning or governance.

sec.title: 9 Limitations and Threats to Validity
sec.p: This manuscript specifies a framework and evaluation protocol; it does not report completed experiments. The 85% threshold is a prespecified target and must not be cited as achieved. A mature full-paper claim requires the benchmark release, executable prototype, baselines, ablations, confidence intervals, and reproducibility artifacts. Until those elements exist, the work is best classified as a framework, methods, or work-in-progress contribution.

Construct validity is threatened by incomplete gold workflows and legitimate analytical alternatives. We mitigate this through multiple gold graphs, invariant-based result tests, and expert adjudication. External validity is limited if tasks, languages, or regions are narrow; geographic and domain holdouts address but cannot eliminate this concern. Internal validity may be affected by model updates, stochastic inference, tool-version changes, and contaminated benchmarks. Frozen artifacts, repeated trials, and temporal splits are therefore mandatory.

Knowledge graphs can encode outdated or contested categories, and formal validation can create false assurance when rules are incomplete. The system must record ontology and rule versions and allow domain experts to override them with justification. Predictive case studies also face non-stationarity under climate and land-use change. Scenario outputs are conditional estimates, not forecasts with guaranteed realization, and their uncertainty must be communicated accordingly.

sec.title: 10 Conclusion
sec.p: GeoPlan bridges natural-language inquiry and predictive geocomputation through a typed, verifiable contract. Its central premise is deliberately conservative: an LLM should translate intent, organize evidence, and compile a workflow, but exact spatial computation and predictive estimation should remain with deterministic, testable engines. GeoPlan-IR exposes coordinate systems, units, time, scale, data lineage, model assumptions, uncertainty, and acceptance constraints before execution. Layered verification and human escalation convert these declarations into enforceable controls.

The proposed benchmark and case studies create a path from an attractive concept to falsifiable evidence. The next step is implementation and preregistered evaluation against direct code generation, retrieval-augmented generation, and unconstrained agents. A successful result would not be a chatbot that produces convincing maps; it would be a system that consistently produces reproducible workflows, detects when it should not act, and supplies experts with the evidence needed to approve or reject its conclusions.

sec.title: Declarations
sec.p: Data and code availability. The benchmark, schemas, reference workflows, and prototype are planned for public release with persistent identifiers after empirical validation. No new empirical dataset is claimed in this framework manuscript.
